learning: If oscillation falls without a progress loss, test 0.9 kg next. If progress falls, mass is not the lever and the remaining gain must come from the controller.
notes: Single-variable mass test: the Builder's 0.8 kg geometry on the iteration-1 controller, unchanged. Compare directly with iteration 1 (mass 0.6, score 114.39).
rationale: Iteration 1 (wheel_track 0.10, mass 0.6, 5 sensors at 12 mm, y 0.03 m, kp 2.5, kd 0.30, base 1.5) is the best measured design at 114.39. Every run in every iteration ends off track, with max_error at 0.061 to 0.068 m against the 0.06 m floor and rms_error at 0.023 to 0.031 m. The sensor tests have bracketed the layout: lead 0.02 m gave 91.8, 0.04 m gave 109.9, 8 mm gave 102.8 and 16 mm with seven sensors gave 65.7. Iteration 4 (mass 0.5, wheel_radius 0.04, base 1.8) raised oscillation to 0.33 without a progress gain, so extra responsiveness is not the answer. Iteration 7 (wheel_track 0.11) cut oval oscillation from 0.282 to 0.259 but cost oval progress (0.471 to 0.416). Iteration 8 (wheel_track 0.09) gave 113.36 and kept progress near iteration 1, so the track width is near its optimum. Mass has never been isolated cleanly. The Builder's entity0 asks for a single-variable test: mass 0.8 kg on the iteration-1 design. I accept that geometry exactly as specified. For the controller I keep every iteration-1 value (kp 2.5, ki 0, kd 0.30, base_speed 1.5, weights [-2,-1,0,1,2], last_direction), so the race measures only the mass effect. Extra yaw inertia from the heavier body should damp the bend overshoot that drives max_error past 0.06 m. The risk is that slower turn response costs oval progress, as the wider track did. Expected: steering_oscillation at or below about 0.28 and oval progress near 0.47. This is an expectation, not a measured result.
